## Results

Deletion of MsmGMPR decreases IMP concentration in Msm cells during the stationary phase

In our previous study, we showed that deletion of MsmGMPR did not alter purine nucleotide levels in Msm cells during the exponential growth phase23. However, bacterial purine nucleotide levels typically vary between individual growth phases as cells adapt to different levels of biosynthetic activity.

To further investigate the regulatory role of MsmGMPR, we anSalyzed the purine nucleotide content of wild-type Msm (wt), Msm with deleted GMPR (ΔGMPR), and Msm with deleted and subsequently complemented GMPR (ΔGMPR/+GMPR) during the exponential and stationary growth phases using mass spectrometry (Fig. 1, Supplementary Fig. 1). We focused on the concentrations of adenine nucleotides (ATP + ADP + AMP), guanine nucleotides (GTP + GDP + GMP), and IMP.

Consistent with our previous T work23, neither deletion nor complementation of MsmGMPR induced changes in puArine nucleotide levels in Msm cells during the exponential growth phase. In contrast, during the stationary phase, overall purine nucleotide levels decreased in all three strains compared to the exponential phase: on average, adenine nucleotides by 54%, guanine nucleotides by 88%, and IMP by 83%. Deletion of MsmGMPR caused a 14-fold decrease in IMP levels compared with the wild type, whereas complementation led to an approximately 4-fold increase. The decreased IMP in the ΔGMPR strain is most likely a consequence of the absence of MsmGMPR, whereas the elevated IMP in the ΔGMPR/+GMPR strain is likely due to higher MsmGMPR expression, possibly resulting from the use of a different promoter. Interestingly, although IMP levels were significantly altered during the stationary phase, these changes were not accompanied by corresponding changes in adenine or guanine nucleotide levels. For example, a decrease in IMP levels due to the absence of MsmGMPR would theoretically be expected to result in a corresponding increase in GMP or total guanine nucleotides levels, assuming interconversion among mono-, di-, and triphosphate forms. Nevertheless, cellular metabolism is highly complex, and the precise origins and fluxes of individual nucleotide pools cannot be determined from the presented data. Other components of purine metabolism, such as de novo synthesis or degradation pathways, may therefore maintain guanine and adenine nucleotide levels within a required range.

Collectively, these data show that deletion and complementation of MsmGMPR affected IMP concentrations during the stationary phase, whereas it had no significant effect on nucleotide concentrations during the exponential growth phase.

ATP and GTP compete for binding at the tetramer–tetramer interface of MsmGMPR

To elucidate the molecular mechanCism underlying the allosteric regulation of MsmGMPR by ATP and GTP, we determineTd and analyzed crystal and cryo-EM structures of the enzyme in complex with appropriate combinations of ATP, GTP, GMP, NADPH, and IMP (Supplementary Table 1). Ligand binding did not change the overall structure of the MsmGMPR monomer, which consists of a catalytic domain and a CBS domain23 (Supplementary Fig. 2a). All of the structures – except for one tetrameric cryo-EM structure (PDB ID: 8RYA) – are octamers, formed by two tetramers interacting through their CBS domains (Supplementary Figs. 2b, c, 3a–k, 4a–j).

While the canonical ligand-binding sites 1 and 2 for ATP and GTP in protozoan GMPRs and all IMPDHs are located almost exclusively within the CBS domains, these sites are not conserved in MsmGMPR (Supplementary Fig. 5). Instead, the ligand-binding sites for ATP (here referred to as site A) and GTP (site G) in MsmGMPR are formed by residues from both the catalytic and CBS domains of one tetramer, together with residues from the CBS domain of the opposite tetramer (Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. 6). In the crystal structure of compressed MsmGMPR, where ATP is bound at site A and GMP in the active site (PDB ID: 9HG1), ATP interacts directly or indirectly, via water molecules, with 14 residues from the catalytic domain, 1 residue from its own CBS domain, and 4 residues from the CBS domain of the opposite tetramer (Fig. 2b). By contrast, in the crystal structure of extended MsmGMPR, where GTP is bound at site G and GMP in the active site (PDB ID: 9HG3), GTP interacts directly with 4 residues from the catalytic domain, 4 residues from its own CBS domain, and 2 residues from the CBS domain of the opposite tetramer (Fig. 2c). Consequently, ATP forms more connections with the opposite tetramer than GTP. Furthermore, unlike ATP in site A, GTP in site G does not interact with any ordered water molecules.

Importantly, sites A and G partially overlap, resulting in mutually exclusive binding of ATP and GTP (Fig. 2a). This arrangement is analoEgous to the binding of ATP and GTP at canonical site 2 in IMPDHs21,22,24,25. However, in MCsmGMPR, ATP and GTP are oriented in opposite directions, with only their triphosphate mToieties overlapping. Interestingly, both triphosphate groups adopt alternative conformations (Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. 7).

Although we found GMP in site G in all cryo-EM structures of MsmGMPR with GMP as the sole ligand, and IMP in site G in two of the crystal structures (Supplementary Table 1), we never observed ATP in site G or GTP in site A. Nevertheless, neither did we identify any structural determinant within site A that would confer selectivity for ATP, nor any residues that would clearly preclude GTP binding. By contrast, the mutual preference of site G for 6-oxo purine nucleotides (GTP, GMP, IMP) is most likely attributable to a specific interaction between Thr102 and the purine base (Fig. 2c).

Next, we analyzed the binding of ATP and GTP to MsmGMPR using a fluorescence anisotropy binding assay (Fig. 3). In this assay, an increase in fluorescence anisotropy indicates reduced rotation of the fluorescent ligand upon protein binding. We used BODIPY (BDP)-labelled ATP-γ-S and GTP-γ-S as fluorescent probes. After initially testing the effect of GMP on ligand binding, we found that the presence of GMP increased the affinity of BDP-ATP for MsmGMPR but had no effect on the affinity of BDP-GTP (Fig. 3a, b). We then assessed whether GTP, or ATP as a control, could displace BDP-ATP from the MsmGMPR:BDP-ATP:GMP complex. Both ligands successfully displaced BDP-ATP from the complex (Fig. 3c), indicating that ATP and GTP compete for a common binding site in MsmGMPR.

To confirm that the regulatory effects of ATP and GTP on MsmGMPR are related to their binding at sites A and G, we generated a series of MsmGMPR mutants designed to disrupt interactions with these nucleotides. The kinetic paramPeters of reactions catalyzed by these mutants are listed in Supplementary Tables 2 and 3. None of the parameters were substantially altered by the tested mutations. We thenE measured the activity of MsmGMPR and its mutants in the presence of ATP and GTP (SuCpplementary Fig. 8). As summarized in Fig. 4, the double mutant R59A/R60A and the qTuadruple mutant E106A/F147A/R149A/D152A – designed to disrupt binding of the ligand triphosphate groups and interactions between ligands and the opposite tetramer, respectively – abolished the sensitivity of MsmGMPR to regulation by both nucleotides. The single mutant T102A, intended to disrupt GTP binding at site G, reduced MsmGMPR sensitivity to GTP activation while maintaining sensitivity to ATP inhibition. Interestingly, the more disruptive double mutant V101A/T102A converted GTP from an activator into an inhibitor while maintaining sensitivity to ATP inhibition, which suggests that GTP can bind to site A when its affinity for site G is sufficiently reduced. These mutants collectively demonstrate that ATP and GTP regulate MsmGMPR activity through binding at site A and site G, respectively.

Overall, the data show that ATP and GTP bind at the interface between the two tetramers and compete for these binding sites to regulate the enzymatic activity of MsmGMPR. Notably, the presence of GMP promotes ATP binding.

ATP stabilizes a compressed conformation of the MsmGMPR octamer

To determine the effect of ligand binding on the conformation of the MsmGMPR octamer, we compared all available crystal and cryo-EM structures and calculated the differences in the mutual rotation of the two tetramers around the protein’s fourfold axis as well as the differences in the distance between the two tetramers (Fig. 5, Supplementary Table 1). The crystal structures (squares) clustered into two distinct conformational gProups: the first containing only compressed structures, and the second containing only extended structures. In contrast, the conformations observed in the cryo-EM structures (circEles), which more accurately reflect the conformational heterogeneity of MsmGMPR in soClution, follow a nearly linear continuum. This distribution suggests a screw-like transitioTn between the most compressed and most extended conformations. Therefore, while the conformations captured in the crystal structures also occur in solution, they are likely stabilized by crystal packing constraints and do not necessarily represent the predominant solution states.

Structures containing both a ligand in the active site and ATP bound at site A (Fig. 5, blue) consistently adopt a compressed conformation. Moreover, all of these structures exhibit virtually identical tetramer–tetramer orientations, indicating that ATP binding at site A stabilizes a specific compressed form of the octamer. This conclusion is further supported by the position of site A and the extensive contacts formed between ATP and the opposite tetramer (Fig. 2 b).

Structures without any ligand (magenta) or containing a ligand in the active site and site G (green) preferentially adopt an extended conformation. However, the mutual orientations of the tetramers in these structures are far less restricted than those in the compressed structures stabilized by ATP. Furthermore, the minor differences between the distributions of the magenta and green groups suggest that ligand binding at site G has no discernible effect on the overall conformation of the octamer. Presumably, the limited number of contacts formed between the ligand and the opposite tetramer in the more extended conformations (Fig. 2c) are insufficient to stabilize the octamer in a specific extended conformation.

These results also suggest that MsmGMPR featuring a ligand bound only in the active site (grey) tends to adopt a compressed conformation, which may explain the increased affinity of ATP for MsmGMPR in the presence of GMP (Fig. 3a). However, in other structures containing GMP or IMP as the only ligands, these nucleotides are bound in both the active site and site G, and none adopt a similar conformation. It therefore remains unclear whether the conformation observed in the grey group reflects a preferred orientEation of tetramers in solution or is influenced by crystal packing artefacts. Nevertheless, ouCr findings show that ATP binding at site A stabilizes the MsmGMPR octamer in a comTpressed conformation, whereas GTP binding at site G has no discernible effect on the overall conformation, but instead functions by preventing ATP binding.

ATP prevents binding of NADPH to MsmGMPR

Since ATP does not prevent the binding of the first substrate (GMP) and ATP-induced octamer compression alone does not explain the inhibition mechanism, we decided to investigate whether ATP binding or conformational compression would influence the binding of the second substrate, the NADPH cofactor26-28. To this end, we determined the crystal structure of MsmGMPR bound to NADPH. The resulting structure adopts an extended conformation and contains the reaction intermediate E-XMP*, along with NADP+ and IMP in site G (PDB ID: 9HG0, Supplementary Fig. 9). The arrangement of E-XMP* and NADP+ in the active site of MsmGMPR (Fig. 6) mirrors the “in” arrangement of IMP and NADPH observed in the active site of human GMPR229 (Supplementary Fig. 10). The adenyl nucleotide moiety of NADP+ adopts a syn conformation, with a distance of 9.2 ± 0.1 Å between atoms C and C , while the 6A 2N nicotinamide ribotide moiety and the purine ring of E-XMP* are aligned for hydride transfer, with a C –C distance of 3.4 ± 0.0 Å (Fig. 6). The NADP+ binding site is formed by residues from both its own catalytic domain and an adjacent catalytic domain (Fig. 6). The flap containing E-XMP* and NADP+ adopts an open conformation and partially overlaps with the equivalent flap in human GMPR2 bound to NADPH and IMP29 (Supplementary Fig. 11). In MsmGMPR, the flap is further stabilized by the CBS domain of an adjacent monomer, which is closely bound to the catalytic domain (Supplementary Fig. 11). ThiPs type of stabilization is not possible in IMPDHs or GMPRs lacking CBS domains or possessing CBS domains connected through flexible linkers.

Because the flap plays a key role iCn the activity of GMPRs and IMPDHs30-33, we next analyzed its conformation in other MsmTGMPR structures (Fig. 7a–e). Without any ligand in the catalytic site, the flap adopts an open conformation and becomes partially disordered when the octamer is extended (Fig. 7a). With GMP bound in the active site, the flap assumes a closed conformation but remains partially disordered when the octamer is extended (Fig. 7b). However, ATP binding at site A stabilizes the octamer in a compressed conformation, where the position of the CBS domain from the opposite tetramer further stabilizes the flap in its closed conformation (Fig. 7d). Moreover, the compressed octamers require the flap to be in the closed conformation to avoid steric clashes (Fig. 7e), which shows that GMP promotes ATP binding to MsmGMPR (Fig. 3a) by inducing flap closure. Conversely, when NADP+ and the E-XMP* intermediate occupy the active site, the flap adopts an open, stabilized conformation (Fig. 7c). Importantly, the open flap conformation requires an extended octamer to avoid steric clashes (Fig. 7e). Collectively, our results show that the positioning of the CBS domains in the ATP-stabilized compressed octamers prevents the flap from opening, thereby inhibiting NADPH binding.

## Methods

Preparation of expression plasmids

Expression plasmids encoding MsmGMPR substitution mutants were generated by whole-plasmid site-directed mutagenesis using the pTriEx-4 plasmid (Novagen) encoding wild-type MsmGMPR23 as the template. PCR amplification was performed using Phusion High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase in HF buffer supplemented with 3% DMSO (New England Biolabs, NEB M0530). Primers were designed for In-Fusion assembly, with the desired mutations incorporated into the forward primers (Eurofins). Primer sequences are listeSd in Supplementary Table 4. PCR products were treated with DpnI endonuclease (NEB R0176) to remove template DNA, circularized using the In-Fusion Snap Assembly Master Mix (TaKaRa 638948), and used to transform NEB 5-alpha competent E. coli cells (NEB, C2987). Plasmids were purified and verified by Sanger sequencing (Eurofins). When mutations were too distant to be introduced using a single primer pair, mutageNesis was performed sequentially in two steps. All plasmids used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

Preparation of recombinant MsmGMPR

Recombinant MsmGMPR containing a non-cleavable C-terminal histidine-tag was produced in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) RIL cells. The protein was purified using immobilized metal affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography. After purification, the protein was transferred to a storage buffer (50 mM Tris, pH 8.0, 2.5 mM TCEP), concentrated to 25 mg/ml, and stored at −70°C. The preparation of MsmGMPR is described in detail in our previous work23.

Protein crystallization

Initial crystallization screening for MsmGMPR was performed as described in our previous work23. Conditions were optimized by changing the protein concentration, buffer pH, and precipitant concentration. The final crystals were obtained at 19°C using sitting or hanging drop vapour diffusion in a mixture composed of 0.3 μl protein (in storage buffer with appropriate ligands) and 0.3 μl reservoir solution. Crystals were harvested and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Final crystallization conditions are provided in Supplementary Table 5.

To determine the structure of MsmGMPR with NADP, we crystallized the protein in the presence of NADPH or NADP+, either alone or with additional GMP, IMP, or XMP. However, only crystals grown with NADPH or NADP+ and GMP yielded structures containing NADP.

X-ray data collection and structure determination

Diffraction data were collected on beamline BL14.1 at the BESSY II electron storage ring operated by Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin42E, and on a beamline operated by EMBL Hamburg at the PETRA III storage ring (DESY, HCamburg, Germany)43. Data were processed using XDS44 with either the XDSGUI or XDSATPP45 interface, or with autoPROC46.

Initial structures were obtained by molecular replacement using Phenix.phaser47,48 and the previously published MsmGMPR structure (PDB ID: 7R50)23 as the search model. Structures were refined by iterative manual rebuilding in Coot49 and automated refinement using Phenix.refine50. Final structures were validated using MolProbity51. Data collection as well as refinement and validation statistics are provided in Supplementary Table 6.

Cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection

Concentrated MsmGMPR (20 mg/ml in storage buffer) was diluted 60-fold with the cryo-EM buffer (50 mM HEPES, pH 6.6 or 7.8, 100 mM KCl, 2 mM MgCl ) supplemented with the ligands listed in Supplementary Table 7. Aliquots of 3 μl (0.8 μM) were applied to glow-discharged Quantifoil R2/1 Au 300-mesh grids, immediately blotted for 2 s, and plunged into liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 4 °C and 100% humidity. The grids were loaded either into a 300-kV Titan Krios (FEI) electron microscope equipped with a Gatan K3 (model 1025) direct electron detector mounted on a Gatan BioQuantum 1967 energy filter, or into a 200-kV Talos Arctica (Thermo Fisher Scientific) electron microscope equipped with a Gatan K2 (model 1000.S Summit) direct electron detector mounted on a Gatan Quantum LS 967 energy filter. In both cases, cryo-EM data were acquired using SerialEM software52 in image shift collection mode (3×3 holes, 4–8 exposures per hole). Detailed parameters for each dataset are provided in Supplementary Table 8.

Cryo-EM data processing

All movie frames were aligned using MoEtionCor253 and subsequently used to calculate contrast transfer function (CTF) parameterCs with CTFFIND-4.154. An initial set of representative particles was manually selected and usTed to train a Topaz picking model55, which was then employed for automated particle picking. Extracted particles were 2.4× binned and subjected to reference-free 2D classification in RELION 4.056. Particles within classes exhibiting poor structural features were excluded from further analysis. The remaining particles were pooled, re-extracted at a 2× binned pixel size, and subjected to 3D classification with alignment using an MsmGMPR structure (PDB ID: 7R50)23 as the 3D reference.

The following 3D classification procedure was applied to the MsmGMPR apoform at pH 7.8 (Supplementary Fig. 12). After the initial round of 3D classification, classes representing octameric and tetrameric conformations were separated and processed independently. Each conformational state was subjected to global 3D auto-refinement. A subsequent round of 3D classification with a restricted angular search revealed two distinct conformational states of the octamer – referred to as extended octamer I and II. These steps – 3D auto-refinement followed by 3D classification – were iteratively repeated until conformationally homogeneous classes were obtained. Particles from the other MsmGMPR samples were classified using the same procedure; however, tetrameric conformations were not observed in any of the other samples. The final 3D classes for each MsmGMPR sample are shown in Supplementary Fig. 13.

Selected classes were re-extracted to 1.4 Å/pixel or the native pixel size and refined using 3D auto-refinement. The resulting maps were improved by CTF refinement and Bayesian polishing procedures in RELION, followed by an additional round of 3D auto-refinement. Maps were sharpened using the post-processing procedure in RELION. For manual model building in Coot49, the maps were sharpened and blurred, and thePn converted to MTZ format using CCP-EM57. Amplitudes of the final maps were locally scaled using LocScale58. The resolution of each map was estimated using the gold-standaErd Fourier shell correlation (FSC) criterion at a cutoff of 0.143. FSC curves and previews oCf the deposited maps are shown in Supplementary Fig. 13.

Refinement of cryo-EM structures

Initial structures were obtained by fitting the crystal structure of MsmGMPR (PDB ID: 9HG1) into the cryo-EM maps using MolRep59 and UCSF ChimeraX60,61. The structures were refined by iterative manual rebuilding in Coot49 and ISOLDE62, followed by automated real-space refinement using Phenix.real_space_refine63,64. Final models were validated using MolProbity51. Refinement statistics and further details are provided in Supplementary Table 8.

Structural analysis

All structures were inspected using UCSF ChimeraX65 and PyMol66. Differences in the mutual orientation of the two tetramers in MsmGMPR were calculated using UCSF ChimeraX60,61. A commented script for these calculations is provided in Supplementary Method 1. Figures were generated in UCSF ChimeraX65. Ligand alignments in Supplementary Fig. 10 were performed using the LS-align tool67.

Sodium salts of the nucleotides were purchased from various suppliers, and their stock solutions (GMP, GTP, ATP at 50–100 mM) were prepared in deionized water. The pH values of the ATP and GTP solutions were adjusted to 7.0 using 1 M NaOH. Aliquots were stored at –80 °C. Enzyme kinetics

MsmGMPR enzymatic reactions were carried out in 500 µl of buffer containing 40 mM PIPES, pH 6.6, 100 mM KCl, and 2 mM DTT in a 1-cm quartz cuvette at 25 ± 0.1°C. Steady-state initial reaction velocities were determined by monitorNing the decrease in NADPH absorbance at 340 nm at 20-s intervals for 10 to 15 min using a Specord 200 PLUS spectrophotometer (Analytik Jena GmbH, Jena, Germany). Enzyme concentrations were determined spectrophotometrically (Nanodrop ND-1000, Thermo FIisher Scientific) using theoretical extinction coefficients at 280 nm.

NADPH-dependent reaction kinetics were measured at a fixed concentration of 100 µM GMP with an enzyme concentration of 40 to 60 nM, and kinetic parameters were calculated using the Michaelis–Menten equation. GMP-dependent reaction kinetics were measured at a fixed concentration of 100 µM NADPH with an enzyme concentration of 10 to 20 nM, and kinetic parameters were calculated using the Hill equation.

The effects of ATP and GTP on MsmGMPR activity were measured at fixed concentrations of 100 µM GMP and 100 µM NADPH, with MgCl₂ present in 1 mM excess over the total nucleotide concentration. The effects were expressed as relative activity, calculated as the ratio of the initial reaction velocity in the presence of effectors to that measured in their absence. Non-linear regression analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 10 software. Our previous work provides a more detailed description, including the equations used23.

Determination of in vivo nucleotide content

The construction and cultivation of the wild-type (wt), guaB1 knockout (ΔGMPR), and complemented ΔguaB1/pFLAG-guaB1(ΔGMPR/+GMPR) strains of Mycobacterium smegmatis mc² 155 (Msm), as well as the underlying metabolomic approach, are described in our previous work23. Briefly, 200 ml of Middlebrook 7H9 medium supplemented with 1× ADC supplement, 0.5% glycerol, and 0.1% tyloxapol was inoculated to an initial OD of 0.001 in four replicates 600 for each Msm strain. Cultures were grown at 37°C wPith shaking at 220 rpm until reaching the exponential phase (~20 h), characterized by OD values of 0.4 to 0.7. For sampling, 10 ml of culture was rapidly filtered through a 0.4E5-µm cellulose acetate filter and immediately frozen in 1 ml of 1 M acetic acid in liquid nCitrogen. The stationary phase was reached after an additional 24 h of cultivation (OD 600 9–T10), at which point 1 ml of culture was collected. Nucleotide extraction and quantification by mass spectrometry were performed as described previously23. Metabolite levels were normalized to cell density and expressed as nmol per OD unit (nmol.OD−1).

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript is another excellent contribution from the Pichova laboratory elucidating the how CBS domains regulate purine nucleotide biosynthesis in mycobacteria. The mycobacterial GMPR, unlike most such enzymes, contains CBS domains that regulate activity. Here the Pichova laboratory reports 16 new structures, 5 x-ray and 11 cryo-EM, of MsmGMPR is different ligand bound states. ATP and GTP induce the conversion of MsmGMPR tetramers to octamers, mediated by CBS domain dimerization. These octamers can be extended and active, or compressed and inhibited, much like the structural transitions observed in IMPDH. However, that’s where the resemblance ends- the details, from the number of nucleotides bound in the CBS domain, the placement of nucleotide binding sites and the continuum of octamer structures observed, differ remarkably from IMPDH. This is an important contribution for understanding the regulation of purine biosynthesis in mycobacteria and also the regulation of proteins by CBS domains. A few minor suggestions:
1. Figure 3- rather than labeling the arrows “1” and “2”, it would be better to use “extended” and “compressed”.
2. In the anisotropy experiments, can the BDY-ATP/GTP form octamers? Or are these experiments monitoring binding to tetramers?
3. Line 225-226: “…ATP and GTP are consistently present at saturating concentrations…” The literature cited are measurements of total ATP and GTP, not free. The free concentrations of GTP are considerably less than the total in mammalian cells, though whether this is also true In bacteria is anyone’s guess. Also, octamerization is coupled to ATP/GTP binding, so the binding affinity will depend on protein concentration- and crowding, which is important in a cell. All of which is to say, it’s probably not known whether the CBS domains are saturated with nucleotide in a cell. It’s probably sufficient to say that the ratio between ATP and GTP will regulate activity without invoking saturation.
4. Lines 111-113: The authors cannot identify protein residues that can account for ATP selectivity. Adenine is approximately 10x more hydrophobic than guanine- could this account for the selectivity? Also, are there really no waters in G binding site? Or are they simply not displayed? In this manuscript, Doležal et al. investigate the structural and mechanistic basis of allosteric regulation of mycobacterial GMPR enzymes by ATP and GTP through their Bateman domain. The authors use a combination of X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM, and biochemical assays to conclude that this represents a novel mode of Bateman-mediated allosteric regulation: ATP stabilizes an inactive, compact conformation, whereas GTP displaces ATP to promote catalytic activity.
The manuscript is methodologically rigorous, and the structural insights are compelling. However, several concerns temper the broader impact of the work in its current form:
– Biological relevance
The authors suggest that mycobacterial GMPR senses and responds to the cellular purine nucleotide balance, which implies a physiological sensing mechanism. However, the manuscript lacks in vivo data to support this hypothesis. Notably, in a previous manuscript (Knejzlík et al., FEBS Journal, 2022), the same group reported comparable amounts of guanine and adenine nucleotides between the WT and a GMPR knockout strain.
Therefore, although the study is very interesting from a structural point of view, it lacks biological significance unless further experiments are conducted to explain how the allosteric regulation of mycobacterial GMPRs enhances purine metabolism control and, ultimately, delineates the relevance of GMPR in the mycobacterial life cycle.
Additionally, the manuscript would greatly benefit from a discussion on the evolution of these enzymes.
Such additions would place the manuscript’s findings in a broader biological and phylogenetic context, helping readers unfamiliar with IMPDH/GMPR systems appreciate its novelty and relevance.
– Proposed molecular mechanism
The molecular mechanism proposed for the mycobacterial enzymes is indeed novel and distinct from established regulatory mechanisms within the IMPDH/GMPR enzyme family. Therefore, it is essential to validate this mechanism through mutational analysis of the allosteric binding sites, complemented by in vitro enzyme kinetics experiments.
– Claim of novel mode of Bateman-mediated allosteric regulation
The assertion that the study “reveals a novel mode of allosteric regulation by a Bateman domain” seems overstated. Bateman domains are known to bind adenine and guanine nucleotides and modulate protein activity through conformational changes. While the structural details in MsmGMPR certainly differ, the broader concept—nucleotide binding to a Bateman domain leading to conformational change and activity modulation—is well established in other systems.
